utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to everyone, and we resume our work in the usual manner by having the appearances entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for Stanisic Defence Slobodan Zecevic and Slobodan Cvijetic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, appearance from Zupljanin Defence Dragan Krgovic for counsel. Our client sent over their waiver.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I call the witness who is here today, can I just mention in passing, though I would like to discuss it at the end of today, I e-mailed the legal officers and the Defence in respect of the documents for tomorrow's witness. I don't know whether Your Honours were informed about that. And obviously I would like some kind of a ruling or at least some kind of an agreement before he gives evidence tomorrow, because otherwise there are two ways of doing this. One is reasonably quickly, and the other is very, very slowly indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Korner. We have eagerly studied the correspondence, and we hope to be able to rule on it after the break. We will discuss it during the break and then hope to pass down our ruling immediately at the beginning of the second session of today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the witness this morning is Aleksandar Krulj. Your Honours, he is going to deal with a small municipality but which comes under the jurisdiction of the Trebinje CSB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you make your solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, can you please state me your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aleksandar Krulj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Krulj. You can understand me? You have the interpretation? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you tell me your date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 10th of August, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your first name? I forgot. Your first name? Your Christian name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your profession, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am an attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is this the first time you testify before this Tribunal, or did you already testify in other cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm testifying for the first time before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay then. Now you will be asked questions by the Prosecutor first and then in cross-examination by the counsels of the Defence. Okay? Are you okay with that? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I was complaining I hadn't got any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the reason is because I haven't plugged my earphones in. It is Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, can I, first of all, ask you a little bit about your background. I think it's right that you graduated from law school and then worked for the Property Rights Service in the Ljubinje Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Subsequently, did you join the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Socialist Federation -- Socialist Republic, rather, to work as an inspector at the Mostar Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And from Mostar did you move to Ljubinje at the end of 1989 to work on what you've described as the duties and tasks of defence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then in 1991, on the 1st of January, did you become chief of the public security station, the SJB, at Ljubinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you remained there until May of 1994, when you were -- you became chief of the CSB in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just so the Court is aware, you've told them that this is the first time you've testified before this Tribunal, but did you make a statement originally to the prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the State Court?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes. In the case of Krsto Savic and others in February of this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you also testified in the trial against Krsto Savic and others.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes, in March of this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think it's right that a few months ago Krsto Savic and the co-accused were convicted of crimes against humanity.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just so that the Court understands straight away, Krsto Savic, during the period of 1992, was the chief of the CSB at Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I want to move next to asking you a little bit about Ljubinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could we first of all have up on the screen the big map of Bosnia, which is 65 ter 10133. Is there a problem? It keeps coming and going. Actually, Your Honour, interestingly enough we have binders for Your Honours of maps and things that we were going to hand out today and then I left them in my room. We could have used those. Is there a mechanical failure? There's a mechanical failure. All right. No, it's not in ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, if the maps are ready in your office, could you have the scout bring them down to us. Then -- if we need them anyway, we might as well get them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or even a Girl Guide. Can we get somebody to bring them down. I tell you what. I gather it works on video. No, it doesn't. It's stopped. All right. While that's happening, Your Honours, I can go on and ask further questions and then hopefully when we get the things done we can come to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, we'll come back to the maps, because the machinery's not working properly for us, unfortunately. Can we try just one more map and see if that comes up better? 10 -- 65 ter 10062. All right. We'll come back to that. Sorry, Mr. Krulj, you've got it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've got the map, but nobody else has in court, so we'll come back to the various maps. Now, you told us that you started to work in Trebinje in 1989; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: In 1989, I started to work in Ljubinje, not Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ljubinje. Sorry, my fault. And when you became chief in January of 1991, was it still an ethnically mixed police station, SJB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In April of 1991, did you become aware of the division of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I think that the division of the MUP took place in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 1992. Forgive me. In April of 1992. How did you hear about the division of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Well, that would require slightly longer answer. In our area, in Herzegovina where Ljubinje is situated, it's some 90 kilometres from Dubrovnik and 50 kilometres from Neum, the war began on the 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That was the war in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes, but the war spread to the Bosnia and Herzegovina area, to the part of the municipalities of Trebinje and Neum, and this is where regular Croatian Army units were involved. At the time, the security situation was the way it was. In Herzegovina the reserves were called up, the police reserves throughout the whole municipality. War was at the boundaries of our municipality. And I found out about the division of the MUP after a decision by the National Assembly -- or the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska, or the then Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: -- in March 1992 when the government was formed and certain ministries, including the Ministry for Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you sent or did you receive a copy of a letter from Momcilo Mandic explaining about the split of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I don't remember the letter, but if each public security station received it, probably I received it as well. I don't remember the contents, but if I can recall correctly, Momcilo Mandic was the justice minister in that government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. He later became that. All right. On the 1st of April, was there a meeting held in Trebinje, which was attended by all the chiefs of the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that meeting attended by Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware at a stage that he was the new minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Well, I found out about it that day, because they said that new minister of internal affairs was coming, Mico Stanisic. That was the first time that I saw him in my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. At the meeting what did he say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I think that the meeting didn't last that long. Perhaps less than an hour, because the minister was in a hurry to get somewhere. He just informed us briefly that a new Law on Internal Affairs has been adopted of the then Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the provisions of the law are practically identical to the previous one, then the fact that some other existing centres for informing another one was being introduced in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note there is a background noise making it difficult to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you say that some other existing centres for informing was being introduced in Trebinje. Before April of 1992, had there been a CSB in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where was the -- which CSB covered the area of Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: The Mostar Security Centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And was there an explanation from Mico Stanisic why there was going to be a change?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I said that earlier, that the People's Assembly -- well, it was probably -- you know that at the time the National Assembly split up, that the Assembly government and ministries were formed, and I knew that from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. It's my fault. There hadn't been a CSB at Trebinje until then. Were you being told that there was now going to be a CSB at Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: This was written in the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was there an explanation as to why it would longer be in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that. The question is not clear to me. A law was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But was there any explanation given to you why instead of the CSB being in Mostar it was now going to be in Trebinje and that's why -- and there had been a change in the law? Were you -- were you -- was it explained to you why there'd been this change in the law?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I can give you my opinion, because already at the time the majority of the Serb cadres were expelled from Mostar, and they came to the Trebinje area. Not only the employees of the MUP but just regular citizens, people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So had the employees of the MUP from Mostar, or from the centre at Mostar, come to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes. Jovo Cokorilo was the head of the criminal investigations unit in Mostar, and he worked in Trebinje. Zorica Sarenac was the administrative legal advisor in -- in Mostar, and she continued to work on the same job in Trebinje. Marko Cabrilo also performed his duties both in Mostar and in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, when we get the screen back, I'm going to ask you to look at a diagram of the CSB in Trebinje, but at a meeting on April the 1st, were you told who the new chief -- or who the chief of the CSB in Trebinje was going to be?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I think that it was said that it was Krsto Savic, but I don't know whether Krsto Savic got the letter of appointment or not within the next few days after that. I don't know, but it was said that he would be the chief, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you know Krsto Savic before this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes, for a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where had you known him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Well, I met him in Nevesinje. I think that at the time in 1989 he worked -- or while I was still working in Mostar, and he was deputy commander at the time. Ibro Feriz was commander and he was deputy commander, and that was his first job in the police force. And since I was police inspector, I used to know these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, after April the 1st in your police station in Ljubinje, was there a change of uniform?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What, none at all?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Just a change of insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And the change was -- was what in the insignia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Well, the insignia was changed. Instead of a five-pointed star on the cap, they had a tricolour flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did your police officers have to take any kind of oath to the new government, the Serbian republic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think that the formal oath was first done in Trebinje. And as for people doing this in police stations, no. We used to sign an oath always, whenever we were issued with an official ID, rather, that was regulated by the Law on Internal Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina. When a person was given an official ID, then members would give a solemn declaration where they would take up certain duties and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, now I see we have here the actual folders. I don't know if the equipment is working yet, but as I see there's still a technician probably not. Can we hand to Your Honours -- there are two different ones. These were provided to the Defence last week, and we've got them for the court staff as well, or legal officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. It was my understanding that the Office of the Prosecutor provided us with this courtesy copies last week in order that we give some comments before it is provided to the Trial Chamber. I'm afraid since we are very pressed with the witnesses this week, very important witnesses, we didn't have time to give our comments on this. So I'm not opposing that this be given to the Judges, but I reserve the right to comment, if I may, later on. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I say that they're just -- they contain maps. One of them contains maps, and the other contains the diagrams that are attached to the pre-trial brief, but obviously if there's any changes that need to be made we'll take them away and make those changes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've provided them in hard copy, but just in case Your Honours possibly wanted to make any sort of markings. There's two different ones. One is maps, and the other one is diagrams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Without more, I could understand the Defence wishing to reserve the right to make comments about the charts binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They're the ones, Your Honour, that were attached to the pre-trial brief which were altered after the Defence had and input, but as I say, if there's any problem, we can always change it. Okay. Can we -- I'm told the screens are now working, so perhaps for the purpose of the witness we can have up the map of -- the map of Bosnia, please, which is 0 -- 10133. Yes. Now, can we move -- it will have to go up a bit because I want the bottom part of the map. Thank you. Stop, stop, stop. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Krulj, I think we can see Trebinje marked at the -- near the bottom tip of Bosnia, if I can put it that way, and we see Dubocanin just to the left of it, and as you pointed out to us, Montenegro is to the right as we look at it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Ljubinje, which is where you were based, if one goes up the map from Trebinje towards Stolac --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes. Sixty kilometres to the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And just while we've got the map open there, Bileca, which was another municipality that came within the jurisdiction of the CSB Trebinje, is to the right of Trebinje, looking at the map, and virtually on the border with Montenegro; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes. Thirty kilometres to the north of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then -- I don't have Gacko marked, but I can't see it at the moment. Oh, yes, Gacko. One goes up the border from Bileca, going up the map. Gacko is a little bit further up to the -- to the right; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Forty-four kilometres to the north of Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite right, to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then can we have the next map on the screen, which is the second map in the bundle. 10134.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And that gives us a clearer idea of the municipalities. We see Ljubinje, and as you talked about, there's Neum to the west and Bileca to the east, and then Stolac and --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: To the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To the west. Right. Finally on maps, can I ask you to look, please, at an ethnic map of Ljubinje, which is number 10062, which you had a chance to look at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's not in Your Honours' bundle. If we -- can we see the top of the map first of all, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This shows the -- your -- the municipality of Ljubinje with markings showing the ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's fairly clear so we haven't bothered to translate it. It's a map based on the census of 1991, Hrvati being Croats, Srbi being Serbs, and Muslimani being Muslims, fairly obvious, and those that describe themselves as being Yugoslavs and then others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, you had a chance to look at this map. Do you agree that it's an accurate representation of the way the -- the various villages were made up ethnically in the area of Ljubinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes. And I agree, and I'm familiar with this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it appears that the only majority Croat village was a small one called Misljen.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes, Misljen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we can see that in fact the Serbs in this municipality had an absolutely overwhelming majority; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There appear to be only 39 Croats on some 332 Muslims in 1991. In 1992 were the figures still the same more or less?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Which month?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: All of the Croats remained in the territory of Ljubinje, and some Muslims moved away in July of 1992 to Montenegro and to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now finally on diagrams, could you have a look, please, at a pictorial representation of the CSB in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's in Sanction, and it's in the second binder, Your Honours. I think it's 610. 611. Sorry, it is number 11. It's the last document in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. First of all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The chief is shown as Krsto Savic, and we see the chiefs of the SJBs that came under Trebinje, and we can see you. I agree it's not a very good picture of you, Mr. Krulj, but that's you to the very right; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are the chiefs who are shown on that diagram correct? I mean, obviously we know there were changes, but at the time we're talking about it's April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I can say that in 1992, at that meeting, there were chiefs of Trebinje village, Gacko, Berkovic, Nevesinje, and Ljubinje stations. Now, as for the reorganisation, when Foca, Kalinovik, Rudo, Cajnice, and Visegrad were attached, I can't really confirm that it was in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: And there was a mistake here. I think it says -- let me just see. Bosko Govedaric. His real name is Govedarica -- his last name is Govedarica, and as for the others, yes, I'm familiar with their first and last names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, of -- this is Kalinovik SJB, is it? You say there's a mistake in the name.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just spell the last name of that chief for us.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Govedarica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll have to make some changes. Now, was there also working at Trebinje CSB a gentleman named Cuk?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Cuk was acting chief of police department in the Trebinje centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was he appointed early on or later?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: He was commander of the police in charge of traffic security. He had completed only secondary education, and he didn't have an education higher than that, and I think that that's why he was acting chief. That was back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I will just ask -- sorry, it's my fault. When was he actually appointed acting chief? Straight away when the CSB was created?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: When the CSB was created, because police department exists within the security centre. He could not have been appointed earlier than that, because the institution did not exist earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally before we leave the diagram, we see that the undersecretary for national security service, the SNB, first of all, was a man called Slobodan Skipina, and then Dragan Kijac. Did you attend later in 1992 meetings or a meeting with Slobodan Skipina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: As far as I remember, just once. There was a joint meeting in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And underneath that as head of the SNB in the Trebinje CSB was a gentleman named Slavko Draskovic. Did you also meet him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all we need from that diagram. Now, next can I just ask a few things before we look at the documents that I'd like you to assist us with. Was there a Crisis Staff set up in Ljubinje as everywhere else in the area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes. In every municipality there was one, either War Presidency or in some cases it went by the popular name of Crisis Staff, but, yes, they did exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry, because we know they were later renamed War Presidencies. And did you attend meetings in your capacity as chief of the CSB in Ljubinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Chief of the public security station in Ljubinje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I said CSB. SJB. And would you attend those meetings on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: No, not every time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you also attend a number of meetings in Trebinje which were called by Krsto Savic as the chief?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going to look at the records of some of those in a moment, but how often would Krsto Savic call meetings on average during the period April until September of 1992 in particular?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Well, depending on the security situation, but mostly there would be a meeting every 10 to 15 days. Every 10 or 15 days. And maybe sometimes there were meetings that were one week apart.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How would you find out about the meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Communication was a problem with us, telephone communication. We didn't have faxes either. Sometimes we would use radio stations, ultra shortwaves, and we would be notified either by a courier or by telephone, because almost every day somebody travelled between these places, either civilian authorities or somebody else. So we would use that. We would use courier if telephones were not operating. Otherwise, we would use telephone, and we would be notified that the meeting would be held on such and such day at such and such time. They would be mostly in Trebinje or in Bileca. In Trebinje we would hold meetings in the pensioners' centre, and in Bileca it would be in cultural centre, which is used for something else nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can I deal now with communications, please. Were you obliged to send reports to the CSB in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Every police force, even nowadays, all European police forces have regulations on how reports are sent in their chain of command. So we had a regulation that regulated all kinds of reports. It was called an instruction on regular, emergency, and so on reporting. It existed within the ministry. It was in force then, and it is in force even nowadays. Reporting covered some major events. I don't want to go into details, but we would have monthly reports, reports sent every three months, and we would have current reports that were sent daily every day at 6.00 p.m. We would inform about the security relevant events in the municipality, and it would be sent to centre, and then the centre was duty-bound to send a report to its superiors, which was within the ministry. So we would make it for the territory of municipality. Krsto would make a report for the territory of the region, and then somebody else would probably make it for the territory of the entire republic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not sure whether the report was sent at 6.00 p.m. or 6.00 a.m. Could the witness repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Krulj? Could you tell us, was it 6.00 a.m. or 6.00 p.m. that you sent your report, your daily report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I think that at that time it was both in the evening and in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you told us that you occasionally had problems with the telephone. How would you send the reports or the -- by telecommunications, I mean, fax, printer, what?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: It applied only to Ljubinje. It was typical for Ljubinje only. Before the war within the postal and telephone telegraph system Ljubinje belonged to the Mostar area code 088. So physically speaking there was a communications tower facing Mostar and the Velez mountain. When it was destroyed a new one had to be built in 1992, a new relay tower, and then the new one was turned to face another direction. So for about six months we had problems with telephone communications, which means that we did not have fax or teleprinters. So we would mostly send it via courier. At least I would from Ljubinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did you have secure -- when you had telephone, the telephone working, did you have secure phones? Special police secure phones?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: No. We had it before the war but not later on. You mean what we used to popularly call special phones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours line 19 -- page 19, line 12. I believe the witness gave the number of months during which he lacked any communication, and it didn't enter into the transcript, and I would like that this be clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you -- did you -- Mr. Krulj, you were asked if you gave the number of months that you say that the communication tower wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I said perhaps as long as six months. I think while the new relay tower was being built. I wouldn't be able to say whether it was four months or six months, but for a longer period of time in 1992, starting with the destruction of the relay tower on the Velez mountain, which was sometime in late April, and then all the way until the fall. During that period of time. It could have been as long as six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying you had no telephone communication at all during that period or only intermittent? In other words, from time to time.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So all reports had to be delivered by courier every day.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Mostly, but it wasn't an everyday thing. It was too expensive. We used a macadam road that you could only drive 50 kilometres an hour to get to Trebinje, so it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, as it turned out, did you have any major problems in your area of operations, in Ljubinje? For example, with paramilitaries or the like?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: No, but we had a lot of soldiers coming in, because war was under way. The Trebinje road was captured by the Croatian Army, and there was the Podgorica Corps of the then army in our area. There was a lot of uncontrolled firing throughout the town, violations of law and order. Catering facilities would be taken over. I mean, it was a difficult situation. Thank God there were no killings and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you had your meetings, you presumably learnt about the problems that were apparently occurring in other places such as Gacko and Bileca. Did you have anything like their problems?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: We all had similar problems as far as the security situation was concerned, if you're thinking about the things that I was talking about, the security situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll look at it as we look at the records of some of these meetings. I want to just concentrate on some reports that were sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, on the screen 65 ter number 936.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's -- have you got your volume of documents, Mr. Krulj? Could you -- no, you haven't. Somebody's taken them away?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could he have them, please? It's going to be easier if he look -- quicker if he looks at them in the binders. Sorry, there was a binder in front of him. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you go to, please, the first page. It's now on our screen, but -- in other words, the B/C/S is but not the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page, please, of that to begin with. The last -- very, very last page. And for some reason we have B/C/S on both sides of the screen. No. What's going on. We want the last page in English, please, and the last page in B/C/S. No, the last page. No, honestly, you had it up. Last page in B/C/S, please, last page in English. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. This is apparently a document which bears the stamp of the minister of the interior and a signature. Do you recognise Mr. Stanisic's signature or not? If you say -- if you don't, say so.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I didn't really see that many documents with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It's dated -- and if we go to the first page, please, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And English as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That says "Daily report," from the minister of the interior, dates 22nd and 23rd of April, 1992. It's report number 3. Then can we go, please, to the second page in the English, and it's still the first page, I think, in the B/C/S. Does that say -- I think it's the last paragraph, that: "On the 22nd of April, 1992, an explosive device went off in the Centar cafe in Gacko"? Now, two questions: I know you weren't in Gacko. Were you aware from any meetings you had that this had happened, this explosion in a cafe owned clearly by a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Well, I believe that it did happen. It says so in the report, but I don't think that it was particularly discussed at any meeting. I mean, it's not the only thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but it was quite --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: It was the only thing that happened in our area. It's possible that the chief informed us at a meeting that during the past month such and such things happened. That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you say it wasn't particularly -- sorry, I'm just going to turn up what you did say. I don't -- you don't think it was particularly discussed. Was it not there -- wasn't it unusual, therefore, to have an explosive device placed in a Muslim cafe?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Looking at it from now, from this point of view, it is unusual, and it's terrible. At the time, such device were planted under cars, in cafes both on the Muslim and Serbian side, and unfortunately was just a part of our everyday life at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is a report, apparently, from Mr. Stanisic. How would the information from Gacko, in your experience, have got to him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I think that Gacko sent the information to the Trebinje centre. Let me just take a look at the date. Yes. And then the duty operations processed that in Trebinje, and then from the Herzegovina area they sent it to the service in the ministry, and then they compiled the bulletin. It's unusual for the minister to sign a report of -- a daily report. In the station it's not even the chief who signs the daily reports. This is something that's done by the duty officer. So this is why I think this is unusual, but perhaps this was signed by the minister. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we can look at a second example and that's all that I want to. Can we go, please, to 65 ter 938?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, before we leave this document, I apologise for being unable to catch exactly to whom this report was sent. I think it appeared from the top of the document, but I just --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it doesn't say to who it was sent. It just says the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But could we clarify it, to whom this document was sent?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Krulj, to whom this document would be sent?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: As far as I know, we made a bulletin, my service, in order for me to be informed as the chief of the station with all the events during the previous 24 hours. We would send it to the centre so that the chief of the centre would know what would happen -- what happened in the area, the centre covered over the past 24 hours, and then the bulletin would be drafted at the service at the ministry for the minister for his information to know what happened in the territory of the republic. If somebody outside of the MUP requested a bulletin, then it's possible that it was signed by the minister as such a request could be made by the prime minister, the president. In that case, it would be signed by the minister. For your information purposes, internally, that document would be signed by the head of the duty operation service. I hope I was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So presumably the document that was signed by Minister Mico Stanisic, would then be sent probably to the government or to the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our rules, according to the rules of any police force, any document that is sent for information purposes outside of the ministry should be signed by the minister. This is possible. I cannot tell who -- to whom this bulletin was sent. Perhaps to the prime minister, perhaps to the military command if they requested it. This is a regulation of the law on the MUP duties. That's how the procedure goes according to the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may -- may this be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It will be exhibit P155.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And very quickly because I don't want to get too buried in these documents. One other example of Mico Stanisic. If you would pull up, please, 938. First page for the B/C/S and the English. And if you go to divider number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's dated the 24th of April. The first one was dated the 23rd and was marked number 2. This is number 5. And again, if we go to the last page. Second page in B/C/S, third in English. Again, it looks like this -- this one actually is signed for. We see "Za," don't we, for the Minister of the Interior, Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again there's reference to something that happened in Gacko. This covers a number of areas, but if you go to the last paragraph in B/C/S on page 1 and the fourth paragraph on page 2 of the English. We see that on the 23rd of April, a manslaughter took place, and there was an investigating judge from the Trebinje Lower Court. Can we take it from that that investigations into crimes were carried on even during this -- this period of conflict?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may -- that's also on our 65 ter list. May that be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] As Exhibit 156, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, there are a number of examples of these reports but I just want you to look very quickly, if it's at all possible, for one more report, which will be 65 ter 973 behind divider 7. No, sorry, it's wrong. I beg your pardon, 65 -- forget that. That's the one I didn't want to show, actually. It's 65 ter 959, behind divider 4. That shows that it's -- again it's the ministry of the interior, Daily Incident Bulletin Number 15. And if we go, please, to the second page in the English and the bottom of the first page in B/C/S. It says: "No reports or daily incident bulletins had been submitted by Doboj, Bijeljina, or Trebinje, CSB by 1200 hours," 21st of May. What would -- in your experience would be an explanation for Trebinje and indeed the other two not being able to submit reports?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I already said that Ljubinje had problems with reporting back. There were problems with telephone lines because there was no other reason not to send reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And this -- on this occasion it's signed apparently -- or it's not signed but typewritten it says "Investigation And Documentation Service." What was that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: The service for analysis and data. They compile all the interesting events and put them together for purposes of information of the employees. This service was formed in our branch in 1994. It monitors, analyses the situation, the crime rate and the general situation in the area, and then reports back about it. It's a section within the security centre that deals with analysis, and I think -- I hope that it is clear what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... assistance. I note for some time that the witness is talking far too quick for interpreters, and a number of words that he says and parts of the sentences is not entered into the transcript. So if my colleague can please instruct the witness to talk slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, you've heard Mr. Zecevic. If you could try and talk a little bit more slowly so that every word can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, may that be exhibited again. It's on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 157. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is one of about a number of reports which purely go to the communication that was going on. I don't want to waste time by going through every single one of them and it's to be hoped that we can find some method of dealing with these documents either by them going in as a bar table motion or as some kind of agreement about communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can I move next -- oh, well, Your Honours, perhaps -- I note the time. I think it's -- it would probably be better, I'm moving to a different area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have two minutes. Can you make use of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can try to get something up on the screen. That would be useful, I'm sure. I'd like to move, please, to document 96 -- sorry, 65 ter 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you, sir, will find it behind divider 8. This is a report from the CSB at Trebinje, and it's headed "Information on the work of the Trebinje CSB," between the 1st of July to the 15th of August. Now, when you became chief in 1994, would you send these types of reports to the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Not like this unless somebody particularly requested it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what's -- why -- when you say "not like this," what's the difference between this report and any that you sent?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: The information on the work and the security situation in the police is done monthly, every three months, every six months, and annually. Here we're looking at something else. I think that the security situation was quite complex and there were plenty of remarks on the work of the Trebinje Security Centre. So the ministry wanted a report to be drafted for the period of 1st of July to the 15th of August because you can see that it is a little bit unusual what was going on for that period of month and a half. Anyway, that is my opinion of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Would Your Honours like me to go through the content or pause there for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's 10.25. We could take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, the reason for our extended break was that as promised, we are considering -- we have considered, really, your application, and we will give an oral ruling before the Court rises for its next break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, just before we go back to the document that you were looking at and we were all looking at, two matters I ought to have dealt with earlier. Firstly, I forgot to say that apart from your interviews and testimony at the state court, you were also interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor in August of this year, and I think you saw Mr. -- you were able to speak to Mr. Zecevic yesterday; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And one other thing. You were talking about the problem with telephone communication in Ljubinje because of the transmitter. To your knowledge, and if you don't know say so, did the same problems apply to other municipalities such as Bileca and Gacko, or was it only in Ljubinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Occasionally other municipalities would have problems too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you say there was no telephone communication for approximately six months. Was that the same everywhere, or did the transmitter only affect Ljubinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Only Ljubinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we go back very swiftly to this report. If we go, please, in the English to the second page and in the B/C/S also to the second page. Sorry, third page. I see it's got these ridiculous stamps by Mr. O'Donnell. In the second paragraph it states that: "Mostar and Konjic police stations do not function in the area of Eastern Herzegovina, all policemen are placed under the command of units of the Serbian Army. Reserve policemen of Bileca ... 15 active policemen from Stolac ... and 30 policemen from Ljubinje are at the front." And the date of this report -- well, it was a report between July and August. Was that accurate, that you had 30 of your force fighting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we go, please, to page 7 in the English and to page -- it's got 4 at the top in B/C/S, but it's -- 0074-9771 is the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see in the third paragraph: "Frequent cases of unlawful breaking into apartments and moving in represents one of the most complex security problems ..." Was that a problem that affected you in Ljubinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: In Ljubinje we didn't have this problem. We had very few cases of apartments broken into. But I need to clarify something here. This was the period of time when from the Neretva valley, from Mostar and from Capljina, to the borderline municipalities a lot of refugees came to those municipalities, refugees of Serb ethnicity. They had been expelled from Capljina, Dubrava, Stolac, Mostar, and they were the ones looking for some sort of accommodation. If they happened to find a vacant apartment, then they would, on their own, enter those apartments without having a prior decision of the commission for accommodation. So that was what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the empty apartments, who did they belong to? That they broke into.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: In these municipalities, if there were cases of non-Serbs leaving their apartments, then into those. And there were also cases where Serbs had left their apartments, and there were a lot of such cases. People would flee to Serbia or abroad and they would lock their apartments, and these refugees would break into those apartments as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go to the last page -- sorry, the second to last page in the English. And in the B/C/S it is page 5. It's got a little 5, but it's 0074-9773. Sorry, not the last page. Can we go back to the one before the last page in English. Okay. Sorry about this. Forget certified. It's the page before that. Yes, no. No, before. Before, before, before. Page 9 of 12 at the bottom it says, in English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's a list of all of those criminal reports that have been sent in, and we can see that from your municipality it's the smallest virtually. And then at the last paragraph: "For known reasons of nonfunctional judiciary organs in this area reports are not timely filed, although the majority of cases are processed and completed, what will be done." What was the problem about the judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: As I have said earlier, Trebinje was under the jurisdiction of the District Court in Mostar. So there was just the basic court in existence. At the time it was called the Municipal Court in Trebinje, and at that time it wasn't functioning for the simple reason that some of the judges had been mobilised. You won't believe it, but there were -- they were. And as for the judges that I know, I used to know one of them who was a Muslim. He had moved away to Zenica. We still are in contact to this day. His name as Kurtovic Sudo, and I think that that was the reason. So there used to be just two or three judges before the war so that the court didn't start operating right away until new judges came in from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to look at one example of a report that you were involved in but can we ask, please, that this document be exhibited. It's 65 ter 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P158, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you, sir, in your binder go to divider 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we have on the screen, please, 65 ter 10060.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a record of an on-site investigation. The crime was May the 10th, 1992. And if we go, please, to the last page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, the ... sorry, my mistake. Can we -- not the last page in the C/B/S [sic]. It's an on-site investigation -- beg your pardon. Can we have, sorry, the first page. Yes, in B/C/S. That's right. And the first page in the B/C/S. Yes, dated the 4th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is addressed to the public security station Trebinje. The date is actually the 4th of February, 1993, and we see the head of the SJB, Aleksandar Krulj, but the offence was May the 10th, 1992, and what happened was that artillery shells seemed to have damaged the Orthodox cemetery. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you tell us, first of all, why would the date of the report that you sent be in February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I can't remember the reason now. I did sign this criminal report, this criminal complaint. Whether it was only the fact that they were not functioning, I don't know, but I can say that starting on the 10th of April, almost on a daily basis 20 to 30 shells fell on Ljubinje, the inhabited part. So all of the buildings were damaged by the shells, private houses, socially-owned houses, villages, buildings, and so on. If in wartime one were to create such on-site investigation reports and file criminal reports, I don't know if it would be possible, because this was a war area after all. And in this particular case, somebody -- some of the religious officials asked us to compile this report, and we did file a criminal report. And as you could hear just now, the courts were not functioning at the time when this record was made. I gave you an explanation. I don't know. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. All right. On the subject of -- of religious damage, destruction, was there a mosque in the town of Ljubinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I think that during night-time some kind of an explosive device was planted there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was it -- it was planted. Did it go off?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And the majority of it was torn down. When I say a device, I'm referring to an explosive device.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough idea of when that was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I think that it happened sometime in early June, and I think that we have records of that at our police station. I can't give you the exact date, but I think it was early June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So this destruction wasn't the result of shelling but somebody planting explosives. Did you ever find the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see if you could find the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who was if possession of explosives at that time of the -- the events?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Well, the military -- or, rather, the engineering corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there also a Catholic church in the town?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to that during these events of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Nothing. Not a single bullet was fired into that church. It remained intact as it used to be, and now they have added some more to it, so it's bigger now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this wasn't on our 65 ter list, but it's a document that this gentleman dealt with. May it be admitted as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We do not object to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P159, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Krulj, I want to move to a very big meeting that you attended on the 11th of July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 198, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you will find it behind divider number 9 in your bundle. Now, the document is headed "A brief analysis of the functioning of the MUP so far and the outlines of its future activities. (Summary of the meeting of the MUP officials of the 11th of July, 1992)," and it's headed, the Ministry of the Internal Affairs. Can we turn, please, to the second page in both English and B/C/S. Does your name as attending appear in the second paragraph, roughly three lines from the bottom of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the meeting, it was attended by really the great and the good, Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Kljajic, Mr. Skipina, Mr. Kusmuk, everybody and everybody, as we can see. There were very few members of the heads of the SJBs present. Just yourself, was it, and Mr. Cokorilo? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also Mr. Petar Mihajlovic was their from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but do you know why you were asked to attend this meeting, and I should ask you this first: Who asked you to attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Krsto Savic asked me to attend. Since this was a rather serious meeting they needed information on the security situation, so it was up to me to inform them about the situation regarding the police and Jovo Cokorilo about the crime rate and so on. I think that I was invited because, I can say so openly, I was qualified for this particular area. Before the war I used to work as a police inspector. I controlled the work of all police station, Mostar, Neum, Rudo, in the area of the entire Herzegovina and that was my speciality, my professional speciality. So this is why I informed them about the security situation, and it's most likely that Krsto selected me because other chiefs had just started working. They were new to their jobs and they probably weren't as familiar with the topic as I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to what you dealt with in a minute, but if we go in the English to page 5 of 29, and in the B/C/S to the third -- no, sorry, one, two, three, four ... it's 0324-1852 at the top. Stojan Zupljanin was the first to speak. Was he somebody that you knew? Sorry, after Mico Stanisic, rather.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you know Stojan Zupljanin before this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, he made a very, very long speech indeed, and I would like you to have a look, please, at -- and it's the English page 8 at the bottom and in the B/C/S it is page 0324-1855, I think. At least I hope so. Do you see a paragraph, sir, that begins "The army and the Crisis Staffs/wartime Presidencies"? Can you see that in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: " ... demand gathering as many Muslims as possible and leave such non-defined camps to the internal affairs." Now, in your municipality or in any that you knew about from your meetings at Trebinje, were the army and Crisis Staffs demanding Muslims should be gathered together and put in camps which were being run by the police?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: What I see here is that this was something that the army and the Crisis Staffs asked for. I can say that in the territory of my municipality there was no such thing. No population was gathered. There was nothing of this sort. I heard that this happened in Bileca, but I don't think it lasted for a long time, at least that's what I heard, as far as our area is concerned, and it's the first time that I see here that something like that was asked for.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But -- I mean, you were present at the meeting. First of all, I suppose I should ask you, did you get a copy of those minutes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: The security centre received it. I think there was a copy at Krsto's, and I think I read it. All right. But what I'm saying is I saw that then. I found out about it. I found out about these things then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. All right then. I want to go through this fairly quickly because it's a fairly long document and it's bound to be -- come up again. Krsto Savic spoke and gave a -- a rundown on what was happening in Trebinje. Then Mico Stanisic again. Can we come, please, to page 14 in the English, and I think it's page 12 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go down the page in English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Mico Stanisic emphasised that the government was working on a new political territorial division of the Serb republic in order to avoid the previously necessary forms of Serbs autonomous districts and regions and to introduce districts." Now, were you aware of the formation of the Serb autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you in your area -- which Serb autonomous region did you come under in your area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: The Autonomous Region of Herzegovina, or Eastern Herzegovina. I don't remember exactly what the name was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, was there any role played by the leader of the autonomous districts in that area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: As far as the police was concerned, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we move, please, to Mr. Kusmuk. Page 17 in the English, and I think it's page 14 in the B/C/S. I'll just see if I've got that right. Now, Mr. Kusmuk was the assistant minister for police affairs and tasks, and he -- in the second dash in his speech says: "Determining the exact number of policemen who will be exclusively engaged in tasks in their jurisdiction and determining the number of reserve police for the sake of professional work. In connection to that, it is necessary to determine Special Police Units for work from the jurisdiction of the MUP." We're going to look at a number of other meetings you attended where the Special Police were discussed, but by July of 1992, were you aware of any Special Police operating in the jurisdiction of the Trebinje CSB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: There was one unit called Special Police, but this was not under the jurisdiction of the CSB, because the CSB wasn't formed as yet. This was formed by the government of the SAO of Herzegovina, and there were a couple of people who were active policemen. None from my station, though, but the rest of the unit comprised criminals and who knows what sort. They had camouflage uniforms, and they were called Special Unit, but they had nothing to do with the security services centre. And Kusmuk says here that it should be formed the way it was done before the war and the way it's done -- or it's supposed to be done, and these are special units of the police where it is exactly specified what their duties are in peacetime and wartime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, first of all, you say the CSB wasn't formed as yet -- oh, sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honours, there -- the two -- the two terms that the witness used, and in Serbian they're -- they're quite distinct, but they have been -- there is a distinction about the units of the police that he talked just right now and the one which he was -- addressed before, and they're both translated as Special Police Units. Now, I can deal with that during my cross-examination, but I just wanted to put you on notice that there is a problem with -- with that. If you allow me, I will deal with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we should leave it. We'll try and sort it out now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, you're talking about a unit that you say was formed by the government of the SAO. Can you -- what were they called?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Special Unit, Specijalna Jedinica of the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then you talked about another unit that was before the war, which you also called Special Unit. Is it a different term in Serbian from Specijalna?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I will try to explain very briefly. I will try. I worked on these duties, and during the war in the law and also during the war -- before the war and during the war members of the Posebna Jedinica comprised of members of regular and reserve forces from the stations. These are younger people up to the age of 28, and they are used in order to prevent arming in greater numbers, destruction of sabotage groups, assistance when there's some natural catastrophes. During the war these units in the station zone are engaged in combat areas in a specific area. In later organisation, a Posebna Jedinica was established at the public security centre. This unit is headed by an inspector from the police who deals with preparations and defence and heads that unit. There is a unit like that in every -- there are members of that unit from each municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the numbers of the units from the different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're going too fast, Mr. Krulj. How many members are there from each municipality?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: It depends on the number of the police. There were five from some municipalities, ten from others. These were men who were fit to serve on complex assignments. These units still today are used, for example, when there are high-risk football matches. Then the unit would be assembled in Trebinje under the command of an inspector from the centre. This has nothing to do with the Specijalna Policija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I want to concentrate on what you called the Specijalna Policija, the one that was performed by the SAO?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: We have nothing to do with that police. We got a detachment of the Specijalna Policija in June 1993. This was in the area of Trebinje, and it was part of the police brigade, but we had no jurisdiction over that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. I -- I'm not disputing for the moment anything. I just want to find out a little bit more about this unit. This unit, you say it was formed by the SAO. By who in the SAO?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I don't know. The government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And who was the -- do you know who the head of the government was of the SAO Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Vucurevic was the president and the prime minister was Bojovic. I think it was Bojovic. I don't know the first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you said that this unit was formed of -- sorry, can we just go back in LiveNote to -- what she actually said? Right. There were a -- yes. You said there were a couple of people who were active policemen, but the rest of the unit comprised criminals. How -- how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say criminals. I said people who were on the boundary of or on the boundary of the good side of the law. They could be thugs. I explained that earlier. When we worked after those events, many of those in the civilian authority didn't have confidence in the MUP because they believed that we were a remnant of the old system, and this is where we had problems in our operation regardless of how professional we were in the force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, but how did you find out about these Special Police that you say had two active policemen at least?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Well, every time I went to Trebinje I found out. Of course, this unit was discussed, that it existed, that it went to assist here and there in the front near Mostar or Dubrovnik. This is what I know. This was some kind of informal conversation in the town. There was no connection either in terms of logistics or establishment with the Ministry of Internal Affairs. I didn't ask for their services and nobody else did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, but if it had two active policemen in it, how do you know it had absolutely no connection with the Ministry of Internal Affairs? And not too fast, please, Mr. Krulj, because the interpreters are having problems.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Many members of the police left the police force at the time. Some went to the army. Some were in this unit. The unit was not accountable to anybody at the security centre. All I can say is that I heard that it existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: And that it didn't exist that long.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Did you speak to Krsto Savic about this unit to find out what he -- what connection, if any, he had with it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I don't know. We did talk for sure, but I cannot remember. I don't know the connection that he had with it. Perhaps the fact that it was engaged in the Nevesinje front, that could be the only connection, but we did talk about, and it was known that they were engaged at the Trebinje and Dubrovnik fronts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And you said -- lastly, you said that the CSB hadn't been formed. But by July of 1992, there was a CSB at Trebinje, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then finally, can we look at what you said, and Mr. Planojevic. You spoke -- it's our page 18 of 29 in English, and I think you'll find it -- sorry, that's one thing I haven't marked. We see Mr. Nedjus [phoen] speaking, first of all, and then you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's, unfortunately, one thing I failed to mark. Did you find it? Could you just tell us the page so we get the right part on the screen. I think it's -- yes, I see Mr. Nedjus now.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: Sixteen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sixteen. Thank you. When you spoke, Mr. Krulj, you directed, according to the minutes, your speech towards the supply of personnel and the operation of paramilitary formations. Can you now remember, and if you can't, what you were actually -- what your topic of -- what you were raising for discussion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I already said that, that I was invited to the meeting, the topic of which, as you can see, was that the level to which the centre was manned was not even 10 per cent. The police stations also were suffering from shortage of active police officers, people who are familiar with police work. And I can see here that others said that we needed to engage policemen who were refugees from Mostar or Stolac, not even from our -- that we need to accept them in our region and replenish our ranks in that way. As far as paramilitary formations were concerned, I also said that we didn't have any in the area of our municipality. There was a group, local thugs. I don't say they were criminals. They tried to engage units of that sort, but I prevented this. This happened in the Mostar area, I think in Nevesinje. There was a small group. I just reminded myself about that by reading the material. Berkovici. These were units of some kind of volunteer forces who arrived without any kind of command, any kind of equipment, and their only, their sole objective was looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And you say you were able to prevent them, were you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I did that in Ljubinje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened in our municipalities, though, Bileca and Gacko, for example?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I really don't know any details about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to leave that meeting, thank you very much, because other witnesses will talk about other matters. But may it now be exhibited, Your Honour. That was 198, 65 ter 198?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very quickly could you have a look, please, at document behind divider 10, which is 65 ter 992. First page in B/C/S, second page in English. This is a report of the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Second page in English, please. It was along the last meeting. Thanks. At the top. At the top of the page, please. No, that's not -- that's the first -- no, no, it is. Third -- I do beg your pardon. Third page in English. It's my fault. And second page in B/C/S. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the top of the page there, it's the last sentence in the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we bring down -- you've got Trebinje back again, please, in B/C/S, not Bijeljina. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "An increasing volume of misinformation is affecting the political situation in the centre's area by giving rise to anxiety and concern amongst the population." Do you -- do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ
utterances.text: I don't know. This is not an official matter for the police to be assessing the political situation. Perhaps -- and it has to do with the kind of misinformation that somebody of the -- from the politician ranks sold the territory, that such and such forces captured a certain area.
